text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--A majority in the parliamentary group of the far-left opposition Socialist Peoples Party has come out in favour of recommending a 'yes' to the European Union's Amsterdam Treaty reforms in the referendum to be held in Denmark next year, rejecting party leader Holger Nielsen's rejectionist line. The split is seen as putting major pressure on Nielsen.
--Despite the changeable weather with frequent showers, the grain harvest on the central Danish island of Funen, a major growing area, is shaping up well, according to a survey of local farmers.

--Despite the collapse of its alliance with third biggest BG Bank and Topdanmark insurance, leading mortgage credit institution Nykredit is as strong as ever and now poised to enter the private banking sector.
--At least 400,000 Danish mobile telephone subscribers cancel their subscriptions every year, making Denmark the most fickle GSM market in Europe.
--The Danish customs and excise authorities want to set up a controversial computer registration system in its fight against escalating economic crime.

--Danish finance minister Mogens Lykketoft is willing to discuss lifting the share investment ceiling imposed on the country's two biggest pension funds ATP and LD. At present they are restricted to placing 35 percent of investment funds in stock, as opposed to most private mortgage credit firms, where the limit is 40 percent. It is the current rise in the value of shares, which has forced ATP and LD to request a raising of the ceiling.
--Tele Danmark, the Danish telecommunications group, is eyeing the possibility of entering the Far East market, assessing the possibility of participating in tele-consortia in Asia.
